what_would_settle_it: Two checks; the first is a ten-minute canary. In a bypass-mode Workflow, have that agent try to read ~/.railway and ~/.ssh/known_hosts and to run ssh, railway and gh. It passes only if the harness refuses all of them; the model declining on its own does not count. Then run 3 real research briefs through the agent: pass if none drops to tool_status web_unavailable or loses facts compared with an unrestricted run. If deny rules or the agent's tool list are not enforced on workflow subagents, the structural version is dead and only a planning rule remains, which is worth skip. (1) docs/program/evidence/harness-ideas/horthy/README.md rows 18-19 ("`workflows/*.js.txt` | The Workflow-tool scripts exactly as run"). Its manifest.sha256 lists 9 tools/*.txt files and 3 workflows/horthy-sweep-*.js.txt files.
(2) KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN-2026-11.md appendix (~lines 970-971): the evidence/knowledge-store/critique-2026-11-03/ and refute-v1.3/ folders each hold "the workflow script, output and journal (wf_*.*, *.js.txt ...)".

Nothing here reopens a deliberate skip: it is not a hook or the context system, and HR §4 line 275's M00-M06 is an evaluation-run pipeline, not a compliance check. what_would_settle_it: Over the first three phase sessions (P1, P2, P3), run a zero-dep Node script at phase close. Python is not on PATH, and transcripts are pruned after cleanupPeriodDays, so it must run at close. The script filters the main-session and subagent JSONL down to tool_use rows: tool, subagent model, Bash command and exit, edited paths. It scores a fixed list of 8 steps that leave no git/gh artifact as evidenced, absent or undecidable: (a) reviewer subagent ran on an Opus model id; (b) the reviewer brief contains the head SHA; (c) the brief contains register ids; (d) the main session made no Edit/Write outside docs/ (Fable never implements); (e) backend/web/mobile gate commands executed with exit 0; (f) `git diff --stat <sha>..origin/main -- docs/program/` was run on resume; (g) implementers' model ids match the routing table; (h) the closing message carries the six answers. reason: A smaller version survives as a trial: a deterministic, read-only check, run at phase close, of transcript tool_use records for routine steps that leave no git/gh artifact (Opus reviewer, gates run, Fable never edits code, resume diff run). It drops the event-log replay half (refuted, and the PR-body journal already exists) and the "store consulted" criterion, which the KS lookup log and the K24/KS-9 cross-check already cover, for a store that will not exist during P1-P3.

counter_evidence: Dex's case, where a human hand-edits a plan file while the model is still writing it, has no counterpart in this harness, and the only evidence for it is one live anecdote (C1731). HARNESS-REVIEW-2026-11-01.md line 270 already records "one owner per kind of state (plan, PR body, W0-results, git)". OWNER-VIEW.md lines 79-83 gives the owner chat and merging as their channels; it never has them edit the PR body. The ship plan changes only through amendment PRs, and SHIP-PLAN §0 lines 36-39 (`Plan @ <sha>` plus `git diff --stat <sha>..origin/main -- docs/program/` on resume) already catches a plan that another session changed. So a "single writer at a time" rule is effectively already in place. G2-A's new PR-comment channel for owner corrections adds an owner process that the routine does not need. What is not covered: SHIP-PLAN §0 lines 39-41 append the journal with `gh pr edit --body-file`, which replaces the whole body, and no rule says where the text comes from. Two things can lose content as a result. First, GitHub renders the Scope checklist as clickable checkboxes, so one owner click in the UI edits the body. Second, a session that rewrites the body from its own memory after compaction drops entries, which is the very failure HR-C2 has the journal there to prevent. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md has no rule about who writes the PR body.
what_would_settle_it: Showing it worked: when each of P1, P2 and P3 closes, pull the PR body's edit history (GraphQL pullRequest.userContentEdits). Every journal line and every ticked box that appears in any earlier revision must still appear in the final body, unless the journal says where it was moved. Pass means zero unexplained losses across all 3 PRs, plus the P1 cold-resume trial recovering every fact that the journal holds.
reason: Narrowed: the routine has only one writer already (the owner speaks through chat, and the plan changes only through PRs checked by the Plan@sha diff), so a single-writer rule and a PR-comment channel are redundant. What survives is one clause in §0: right before every --body-file write, fetch the live body with `gh pr view --json body` and edit that text, never a copy rebuilt from memory.

counter_evidence: (1) The external evidence is only asserted. In the rpi repo, the 'document-precedence' and 'latest-user-direction' tests check that HumanLayer's own prompt obeys its own order on a toy cap value (1000 vs 2000). They give no error-rate data. The need comes from this harness, not from the source. (2) The harness already has precedence rules, scattered across files: the CLAUDE.md header ("When this file and a prose doc disagree, this file + the code win"); ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md §5.1 CONTEXT block, line 367 ("CLAUDE.md is already injected; trust it"); SHIP-PLAN §2, line 130 ("the Entry line wins if they ever disagree"); and §0 standing rule 5, line 110, which voids the O-08 §4 "503 stub" line inline. §0 lines 36-43 already make the PR journal the home of owner corrections, and the resume step already re-reads changed plan sections. "The user's latest instruction overrides all" is already how chat works, and it gives a cold resume nothing; the journal is what carries corrections across sessions. (3) G2-A's order (owner > journal > Plan @ sha > CLAUDE.md > design note) contradicts two always-present rules: CLAUDE.md's supremacy line (the ship plan is a prose doc under docs/) and the §5.1 instruction "trust it". It would create a conflict between precedence rules. (4) HumanLayer's "most recent wins" relies on a linear chain: ticket, research, design, outline, plan. FixFlow's documents are not linear. CLAUDE.md records the current state (Railway, manual `railway up`), while the plan records the intended state (a VPS host from P3 on). A flat order or "latest wins" therefore gives the wrong answer in one direction or the other. (5) There is a real divergence today that neither reviewer's order settles. SHIP-PLAN §0, lines 86-88, always requires VALIDATE in a later migration after an audit script has run, and cites CLAUDE.md for this. CLAUDE.md itself allows the same migration when the column is provably clean. G2-B's split ("CLAUDE.md over prose for stack facts") would pick the looser rule. A clause saying the stricter rule applies is needed. (6) The benefit on W2 does not exist: a precedence sentence does not make compliance observable. G2-B's measurement (no journal entry records a conflict settled ad hoc) depends on self-report, because a conflict settled silently leaves no entry.
what_would_settle_it: Adopt; the check that it worked uses the P1 cold-resume trial. Plant two conflicts in its frozen fact set: (a) an owner correction in the PR journal that contradicts the Plan @ sha text, and (b) the VALIDATE rule, where the plan is stricter than CLAUDE.md. The fresh Sonnet agent passes if it reports the journal's value and the stricter rule and cites the §0 sentence, 2 of 2. Without planted conflicts, natural ones may never come up and the trial would show nothing. Then, for P1-P3, add one item to each Opus PR-reviewer brief: list every disagreement the diff touches between the plan, CLAUDE.md, the cited design note and the journal, and state whether its resolution follows §0. The threshold is 0 mismatches over the three phases.
reason: Narrowed: adopt one sentence in ship-plan §0, never in CLAUDE.md (W1), split by domain rather than "latest wins": for this phase's work, journal owner correction > plan on main (after the existing changed-section re-read) > Plan @ sha > cited design note; for current stack facts and invariants CLAUDE.md + code win, as they already say; a stricter plan rule beats a looser CLAUDE.md invariant; any other conflict is a stop plus a journal entry, not a guess. It helps W3 only.

counter_evidence: 1) Both reviewers say live watching is "the cheapest compliance evidence available". That is false. Claude Code keeps a full JSONL transcript of every session: C:/Users/User/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl, confirmed for this session as 9c3f9742-d1e5-4e7b-ad89-bb5bcaada06a.jsonl. The transcript records every Read, Grep, Edit and dispatch. So "the store was never consulted" or "the routine was skipped" (W2) can be seen from outside after the fact, for the whole session, without the owner's real-time attention. A live watch covers only ~15 calls and depends on the owner noticing. 2) The harness already has the slot for live catches. Ship plan §0 lines 39-42 keep a "Decisions / ruled out / owner corrections" journal, appended at once. Phase sessions are interactive desktop chats, so the owner can already see and interrupt any tool call. The only new part is the habit of watching on purpose. 3) G2-B's window points attention at the cheapest part of P1. Ship plan lines 322-327 make P1's first act the cold-resume trial: write expected.json, commit it, dispatch a Sonnet agent, judge. The costly wrong turns (Fable implementing, code before the trial is judged, routing errors) come later. 4) The evidence is weak. There are two anecdotes and no numbers. C1532 concerns an unattended Ralph bash loop, which differs from a gated interactive phase. C1685 is a Vulcan CEO's advice, not Dex's. Neither card shows a cost saving.
what_would_settle_it:
Applies to P1 only. The owner watches from session start through the first CODE commit, not just ~15 calls. He writes each departure from §0 into the existing owner-corrections journal. He does not interrupt the cold-resume subagent, so its recovery stays uncontaminated. After close, a fresh agent audits the P1 transcript JSONL against a fixed §0 checklist:
- draft PR opened at the first commit, body starting `Plan @ <sha>`
- expected.json committed before the dispatch
- trial judged and plan fixed before the first code commit
- no Edit/Write to code by Fable
- implementer routing per design §3
- reviewer verdict names the head SHA and fail-before/pass-after per register id
- six-question close
- OWNER-VIEW.md refreshed
Count three things: L = departures caught live in time to avoid rework; T = departures found only by the transcript audit; S = departures the closing message self-reported. Continue live watching into P2 only if L >= 1 and that departure would have cost at least one commit of rework if found after the fact. Otherwise stop watching and keep the transcript audit as the W2 instrument. If T > S, W2's self-report gap is confirmed and the audit, not watching, is the fix to adopt.
reason: Narrowed: as compliance evidence for W2, live watching is beaten by the persisted session transcript, which is cheaper and complete. What survives is a one-off owner watch of P1 through its first code commit, using §0's existing owner-corrections journal, kept only if it catches a costly departure in time that the transcript audit would have found too late.

counter_evidence: (1) C1252's point is the hook form: hooks can apply more expressive, input-value rules than permissions do. Its landing guess, "deny railway up from the repo root", depends on the working directory, which only a PreToolUse hook can see. That reopens the skipped hook category, and HR §6 HR-C5 already flags hook-shell risk on Windows (whether `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` expands). Both reviewers quietly switched to plain `permissions.deny`, which is a default Claude Code feature, not the family's claim. (2) G2-B's "prod-targeted alembic upgrade" cannot be written as a prefix rule. `alembic upgrade head && alembic check` is a gate command (CLAUDE.md Commands; SHIP-PLAN Appendix A backend gates). The prod target comes from the environment, and after P3 `start.sh` applies migrations at deploy. A deny on `alembic upgrade` would block the gate. (3) SHIP-PLAN §0 L61-81: from P3, prod is a VPS deployed by runbook R5 ("owner at SSH"). Railway keeps only the old-hostname hang stub (L519, L636). So a `railway up` rule guards the drain-window stub, and the backend only until P3. The SSH deploy path is not covered at all. (4) The harness has two shell tools, Bash and PowerShell. A `Bash(...)` rule does not gate the PowerShell tool, and nobody has verified a PowerShell rule form. Prefix rules can also be evaded with `npx @railway/cli up`, `bash -c` or `cmd /c`. That makes this a seatbelt against mistakes, not a control. (5) Zero bearing on W2: it makes no phase-routine step observable. (6) C0717's email incident has no counterpart an agent can reach here: the WhatsApp send is server-side, behind `enable_dispatcher`. Its evidence is a single anecdote. (7) G2-A's success metric ("zero such commands executed") would read zero without the rule too, so it cannot be falsified. Supporting the narrowed form: no `.claude/settings.json` exists in the repo or the main checkout, and the user settings hold no permissions, so nothing already does this. HANDOFF L59-63 shows that sessions have run `railway up --ci` and that a repo-root deploy caused a prod outage. This is local evidence, stronger than Horthy's anecdotes.
what_would_settle_it: Acceptance test, run once before calling it adopted. Put the deny block in the project `.claude/settings.json` and run in the same permission mode the workflow subagents use (bypassPermissions). Have an agent attempt four commands: `railway up --ci` via Bash, `cd backend && railway up --ci --service efficient-tenderness` via Bash, `railway up` via the PowerShell tool, and `railway run alembic current` via Bash. It passes when all four are refused by the deny rule and the full backend, web and mobile gate lists (including `alembic upgrade head && alembic check`) run with nothing blocked. If the PowerShell attempt is not refused, add the PowerShell rule form or record the gap in the PR. Then, across P1-P3, count gate commands falsely blocked by the rule. The threshold is 0. It has worked when the four attempts are refused and the false-block count stays at 0.
reason: Narrowed. What survives is not a hook and not an alembic rule: a single `permissions.deny` block with Bash and PowerShell forms of `railway up` and `railway run` (optionally `git push --force`). It cheaply makes a locally recorded outage trap mechanical, which still matters for the Railway stub during the drain window. It does nothing for W2.

counter_evidence: (1) Both reviewers' landing ("named /phase-start and /phase-close skills") duplicates a skill that already exists. The fixflow-orchestration skill (.claude/worktrees/wizardly-hertz-02c46a/.claude/skills/fixflow-orchestration/SKILL.md, commit 1ac6b15, 371 lines) has the description "Use it at the start of every ship-plan phase session (P0a..P14-fleet)". It carries §0 as numbered steps: 2-3 resume (gh pr view, first unticked box, Plan @ <sha> diff), 26 draft PR at first commit, and 35 Close (six questions, OWNER-VIEW refresh, journal entries moved to their owners). fixflow-repo-conventions step 14 repeats the close. Claude Code can invoke every skill by slash command, so /fixflow-orchestration already is /phase-start. (2) The evidence is anecdotal. C1272 says "Personal experience across skills; no counts", and C1268's demo is a trivial secret-passcode skill. That slash invocation loads a skill deterministically is documented tool behaviour that needs neither card. (3) The W2 benefit is mostly illusory. The §0 acts the reviewers would count are already visible from outside without any skill: draft PR timing and the Plan @ line and journal (gh pr view), the OWNER-VIEW.md commit (git log), and the closing message (transcript). what_would_settle_it: Over the first 3 phase sessions, the owner opens with the plain phase prompt and no slash command. From the session transcripts (search for a Skill call to fixflow-orchestration), count the sessions in which Fable loads the skill before its first subagent brief or first commit. The owner may intervene after turn 1 if it has not loaded. If 3/3 sessions auto-load, the description match is enough and no convention is needed. If 2/3 or fewer do, make an explicit `/fixflow-orchestration` the first line of every phase prompt, plus an explicit close prompt naming step 35. Whatever the result, judge close compliance in each session from artifacts, not from invocation: the PR body has the Plan @ line, the journal entries were moved, the closing message has all six answers, and an OWNER-VIEW.md commit exists. Pass is all present in 3/3.
reason: Narrowed: no new /phase-start or /phase-close skills, because fixflow-orchestration (steps 2-3, 26, 35) and fixflow-repo-conventions (step 14) already encode §0 and are already slash-invocable. What survives is a zero-cost habit: invoke /fixflow-orchestration explicitly at phase start, and prompt the close step explicitly, instead of relying on the description match. It guarantees the instructions are loaded, not that they are followed, so it does little for W2; compliance is still checked from the PR and git artifacts.

counter_evidence:
(1) The evidence is weak. All 7 cards are marketing, asserted or anecdotal, and none gives a number. C0270 (humanlayer-pi) is an alpha cloud mirror built for the pi agent, not Claude Code. It uploads tool calls and repo diffs to a third party. C0280's queryable run store is specific to BAML, and building one rebuilds the skipped "Measurement pipeline M00–M06; evaluation-run schema" (HARNESS-REVIEW §4 skip table, line 275). C0242's steering count per PR is a team factory metric, and here the one developer is the only steerer. So the "externally mirror" and "run store" halves are refuted.
(2) Most §0 acts already leave durable artifacts outside the agent, so a transcript is the wrong source for them. SHIP-PLAN §0 lines 24-60 list them: the draft PR at the first commit (PR createdAt can be compared with the first commit), the "Plan @ <sha>" first line, the journal kept with `gh pr edit` (GitHub keeps the edit history), the OWNER-VIEW.md refresh commit, the reviewer verdict naming the head SHA, and docs/program/evidence/resume-trial-P1/ with its sha256 manifest. All of these can be checked with gh and git.
(3) There is precedent: HARNESS-REVIEW §6 already audited its own session transcript by line number (lines 1944 and 2735).
(4) The data exists and greps work. ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<uuid>.jsonl records each tool_use: one session had Bash 498, Edit 207 and Workflow 44 calls, plus 11 `gh pr edit` hits. There are 1681 subagent JSONL files under subagents/. But there are 5 separate EMS-workshop1* slug directories, one per worktree. cleanupPeriodDays is unset, so the default 30-day prune applies, and the oldest transcript left on the machine is from 2026-10-26. The audit must therefore run soon after each phase closes and glob every slug directory.
(5) The reviewers' tests are flawed. G2-A's "any mismatch → adopt" is one-sided. Both reviewers compare against the closing message's claims, but its six questions claim almost none of the §0 acts, so there is little to compare.
The M00–M06 skip reason ("no gain") was about measuring effect, not checking compliance. A one-off grep with nothing installed therefore does not re-adopt that skip.

The plan chose per-decision defaults instead, so it does not stall a 40-phase plan run by one developer. (3) §0 lines 39-43 add the "Decisions / ruled out / owner corrections" journal. A 'proposed/owner-settled' tag would be written by the same agent whose compliance is in question. It is the self-report W2 is about, so it gives no outside check.

counter_evidence: (1) Evidence: C1273 (G2-cards.md line 2622) says the only basis is that the claim was "Relayed from a conversation with Jeff ... informal". It names no model, no window size and no count. Under the owner rules that makes it anecdotal, and both reviewers scored evidence 1. (2) The harness already does the variant G2-A proposes, a fixed token at the end of the closing message. SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md §0 (Resume bullet) requires every phase's closing message to answer six fixed questions: goal, fit, choice, before/after, evidence including skipped counts, and what remains. It then refreshes OWNER-VIEW.md. Fable reads that instruction at phase start, carries it out only at the end, and the owner can see whether it was followed. It is already an end-of-session canary, and a more relevant one than a passcode because it is part of the routine itself. HR-2026-11-01 §4 line 262 adopted it. (3) A per-turn canary is self-reinforcing. After N replies that end with the token, the model can keep producing it by copying its own recent output rather than by still obeying an instruction from early in the context. A hit therefore tells you little, and only a miss is informative. (4) W2: the passcode tests whether one trivial, salient instruction is still followed. It does not test whether the routine was followed or whether the store was consulted. The routine already leaves outside-checkable artifacts under SHIP-PLAN §0: the "Plan @ <sha>" first line, the draft-PR checkbox list, the Decisions/ruled out journal, a reviewer verdict that names the head SHA, and the OWNER-VIEW.md diff. (5) W1: a canary measured at one CLAUDE.md length cannot show whether the length hurts adherence. KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN M-02 already records that adherence falls past about 200 lines, and the trim stays gated on the pilot. Putting the canary in CLAUDE.md lengthens that file. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md lines 90 and 583 say CLAUDE.md (about 7.5k tokens) is injected into every subagent, so the instruction would reach every workflow agent. (6) L2: HR §6 already settles the response. HR-C1 runs one phase per session, and HR-C4 sets an objective trigger: act if a phase session is observed past 500k. For the 1M-window sessions in this repo, 60% is about 600k, which is past that trigger. Below it, a canary that never misses cannot tell "no decay" from "never reached the decay zone".
what_would_settle_it: The only open question is whether instruction decay starts below HR-C4's 500k trigger. Do not test it with a new instruction. Use the close the routine already has. At each phase close from P1 to P3, record the session's context fill (from /context or the transcript usage fields) next to a pass/fail grade of five things: the six-question close, the "Plan @ sha" line, the journal entries, the ticked boxes and the OWNER-VIEW.md refresh. Reopen a canary only if at least one session fails that grade while its fill is below 500k. Otherwise HR-C1 and HR-C4 already cover the case.
reason: G2-A proposed a fixed token at the end of the closing message. That duplicates SHIP-PLAN §0's six-question close, which is already an early-loaded, late-checked, visible test of instruction-following. A per-turn canary is weaker: the model can keep it alive by copying its own earlier replies. It also does not measure whether the routine was followed (W2) or whether length hurts adherence (W1), and placed in CLAUDE.md it would make that file longer and reach every subagent. Its only support is an informal demo relayed second-hand, so the G2-B skip stands.

Line 653 writes the full container log to disk ("the GATE/SETUP/SUMMARY lines are the result"), and line 654 copies the per-gate logs out. Line 652 says "NEVER a second `docker run`". Web and mobile gates (Vitest, Jest) run natively and are fast, so a truncated run there costs very little to repeat. On the claim itself: C1578 is speculation that the source flags as opinion. A no-truncation line would duplicate it. The only gap is an ad-hoc fast test run outside the recipe, which is too cheap to need a rule or a trial.

counter_evidence: (1) Part of the mechanism is already in place. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md line 98 gives Fable the job of "adjudicating conflicting verdicts". That is safe in Kevin Gregory's setting because the incumbent's outputs were accepted in production. It is unsafe here, because medium and xhigh are the same model and are likely to fail the same way. The default-REFUTED brief also pulls both arms toward the same verdict, so agreement can hide a missed CONFIRMED. (3) The card set contradicts itself on this point. G4-cards.md line 348 quotes Dex on his own effort table: "These single runs don't isolate effort as the cause". A single medium-vs-xhigh diff mixes up the effect of effort with run-to-run noise. Without an xhigh-vs-xhigh repeat, the disagreement count that both reviewers propose as the outcome cannot be interpreted. (4) The evidence is one anecdote (C0699: a README example where 28 of 30 agree, with a paraphrased quote) and no failure data. what_would_settle_it: Do this once, inside F034, with no standing golden set. Take 12 frozen refuter or skeptic briefs from the committed evidence folders (the G1/G2 skeptics plus this review's refuters). Each must have a Fable-adjudicated final verdict, and at least 3 of them must have been adjudicated CONFIRMED or survives. Replay each at its frozen SHA three times: xhigh, xhigh again, and medium. Count four things. (a) The noise floor: verdict flips between the two xhigh runs. (b) Medium verdicts that differ from the adjudicated outcome. (c) Repeat-xhigh verdicts that differ from the adjudicated outcome. (d) Items where medium and xhigh agree but both contradict the adjudicated outcome. The disagreement-only shortcut is safe for this repository only if (d) = 0. Medium routing passes only if three conditions hold: (b) <= (c) + 1, no adjudicated CONFIRMED P0/P1 is missed at medium, and medium-vs-xhigh disagreements exceed (a) by at most 1. Hand review applies only to items that have no adjudicated outcome.

The general practice of qualifying a model by "only review disagreements, then grow a golden set" fails here: same-model errors are correlated, one diff mixes effort with noise, and a golden set would reopen the M00–M06 skip.

The one-tick output would erase the skip-aware signal, and fail-fast contradicts the every-gate design. Their cost (about 6k preloaded tokens per spawn, a few dollars over the program) is already bounded by the skills README's 1024-character and 400-line caps and the ORCHESTRATION §7 overhead line. what_would_settle_it: This applies only if the owner trials F034. Write the decision rule in the trial's PR journal before the first run. Build a settled-answer set: at least 10 P0/P1 register items whose CONFIRMED status rests on code (a fail-before/pass-after test or a merged fix), plus at least 5 settled REFUTED items. Run the same refuter brief at medium and at xhigh, 3 runs each. Medium passes only if all of these hold: (a) no settled-true item is CONFIRMED by medium in fewer runs than xhigh confirms it; (b) no settled-refuted item is CONFIRMED by medium in more runs than by xhigh; (c) medium's total tokens, read from each workflow run's reported token count, are at most 0.6x of xhigh's. What survives is a smaller version: a pass bar written before F034's medium-vs-xhigh trial runs, with 3 repeats per arm, results compared item by item against xhigh's own run-to-run variation, and an unknown token count counted as a fail. Without an F034 trial it should be skipped.

counter_evidence: (1) The principle is already in the harness. SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md §0 Routing (lines 53-55) says that for each register id fixed, the reviewer names the test that fails on the base commit and passes on head. It also lists every changed expected value, removed assertion and new skip or xfail, which covers C0874's "restore the original tests" half as a diff-reading convention. Only the mechanisation is new, and no card has evidence on mechanised versus reviewer-run checks. C0797 and C0762 describe Frontier Code with no results. C0573 is Dex endorsing it. C0781 is one HN commenter. All five are asserted or anecdotal. (2) A naive base-commit run makes the benefit illusory. A new test that imports a symbol, endpoint or script added by the patch "fails" on base with ImportError, a collection error, a 404 or a TypeError. The script would certify exactly the tests that test nothing. The check only has teeth for register-id defect fixes on surfaces that already exist on base, and only if a failure counts when it is an assertion failure: pytest `failed`, not `error` or skipped. Jest's equivalent is an assertion failure, not "Cannot find module". (3) The cost is real. Both reviewers' figure of 15 minutes is a guess that nothing measures. ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.md Appendix A uses fixed container names (line 620: fixflow-w1-db, fixflow-w1-gates), and plan §0 lines 28-30 allow one Docker-gate backend phase at a time. So the base and head runs must be serial. The base run also needs its own `alembic upgrade` on a fresh DB, a worktree needs `core.longpaths` on Windows, and mobile needs node_modules in the worktree (or an in-place revert of non-test files). (4) The benefit on W2 is narrower than claimed. W2 is about main-session compliance: whether the store was consulted and whether the routine was skipped. This check covers one reviewer claim. (5) No deliberate skip is reopened. HR §4 row 272 (the pre-commit verification hook) is a commit-time hook, and the doctor script (row 276) is unrelated. HR line 57's "conventions, not machinery" was aimed at the owner's Python tooling, hooks and checkpoints, not at this check. The plan already adds small scripts where they are needed, such as P1's CLAUDE.md-head CI step. KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN has no fail-before mechanism (no match for those terms). (6) Both reviewers' pass rule ("agrees with every reviewer claim, or catches one false claim") passes on every outcome. It measures feasibility, not benefit.
what_would_settle_it: Run it on the first 3 PRs that fix at least one register id, with at least one backend PR run through the Appendix A Docker gate. Use the plan's own phase sessions, not a new pilot. The script works in a worktree at the base SHA, or reverts the non-test paths in place. It runs each reviewer-named test on base and on head, and classifies each base outcome as assertion-fail, error/collection, pass or skip. It also runs base's version of every modified test file against head. Count four things. (a) Ids where the base outcome is not assertion-fail, or the head outcome is not pass. (b) Head failures of base-version tests that are missing from the reviewer's list of changed expectations. (c) False alarms: script flags that Fable finds to be wrong once it inspects them. (d) Unattended wall time per PR on this Windows machine, plus any manual step. Adopt it as required reviewer evidence, with output committed under docs/program/evidence/ in the sha256 manifest, if all 3 PRs run unattended in 15 minutes or less with 0 false alarms. Drop it if any run needs a manual step, takes longer than 15 minutes, or produces more than 1 false alarm. Each confirmed (a) or (b) hit is a reviewer error caught. Record the count either way; it is the only evidence of benefit.

In that story HumanLayer reviewed "plans and tickets but not code" (C0562), with no independent reviewer of any kind. C0634, from the same author, says real lights-off factories gate on linters plus a second model's review. FixFlow already has both: SHIP-PLAN §0 Routing gives every PR an Opus reviewer that tries to refute by default, ties the verdict to the head SHA and names a test that fails before and passes after for each fixed register id; CI runs three jobs plus import-linter and ESLint boundary checks. So the anecdote never shows what a human read adds on top of model review plus tests. The only measured card, C0714, compares careful review against no review at all. Its own author calls it "a mountain of asterisks", and it counts slop density, not defects. C1261, C1262 and C1280 are predictions. (2) W1 gets nothing: an owner read does not touch the length of CLAUDE.md. (3) The W2 benefit is smaller than claimed. An "owner read" journal line is still self-reported. Against the family (it does fill a real gap): a search of SHIP-PLAN, OWNER-VIEW and ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN for an owner who reads diffs or merges code PRs found nothing. 6. The upstream evidence is anecdotal. C0184 only asserts "thousands of warnings", and that problem comes from oxlint's no-explicit-any warnings.
7. Native web and mobile gates are the only gap. §0 says they "run natively" but gives no output rule. Their commands are `eslint .`, `prettier --check .`, `vitest run`, `vite build`, `tsc --noEmit` and `jest` (package.json lines 12-19; technician-app/package.json lines 10-11). tsc and eslint print nothing on success when there are no warnings, prettier prints about one line, and vitest and jest print about one line per test file. Covering that gap means copying the §4.3 rule into §0, not adopting a new wrapper.
8. One correction to G4-B: its "bash plus PowerShell" cost is overstated, because a Node .mjs runner would work on all three shells. This does not change the verdict.
what_would_settle_it: The one open question is native web and mobile gate output. Check it before the first web or mobile phase (P2a). Run once with output to a file: `npm run lint`, `npm test` and `npm run build` at the repo root, then `npm run typecheck` and `npm test` in technician-app. Count the characters of each successful run (`wc -c`). If any single gate prints more than about 8,000 characters on success, add one line to SHIP-PLAN §0: native gates follow ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN §4.3's output rule (log to scratchpad, report exit code plus failing tail). Otherwise do nothing. Neither outcome needs a run_silent script.
reason: The harness already does this. Backend gates run through Appendix A's per-gate logs and GATE EXIT lines, §4.3 sets an output rule for command agents, and Fable never runs gates. A wrapper silent on success would also hide skip counts that the §0 closing message and P1's skip-aware gate need. The only gap is native web and mobile output, which a one-line §0 rule would cover if measurement shows it is large.
